'''Joseph-Émile Barbier''' (1839–1889) was a French astronomer and mathematician,<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor|id=Barbier|title=Joseph Émile Barbier}}</ref> known for [[Barbier's theorem]] on the perimeter of [[curve of constant width|curves of constant width]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Ren | first = De-lin
 | isbn = 978-981-02-1107-3
 | page = 7
 | publisher = World Scientific, 1994
 | title = Topics in Integral Geometry
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=5MgePUVWXioC&pg=PA7| year = 1994
 }}.</ref>

Barbier was born on 18 March 1839 in [[Saint-Hilaire-Cottes]], [[Pas-de-Calais]], in the north of [[France]].
He studied at the [[Colleges of St Omer, Bruges and Liège|College of Saint-Omer]], also in Pas-de-Calais, and then at the [[Lycée Henri-IV]] in [[Paris]]. He entered the [[École Normale Supérieure]] in 1857, and finished his studies there in 1860,<ref name="mactutor"/> the same year in which he published the paper containing his theorem on constant-width curves.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Barbier | first = E.
 | journal = Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées | series = 2<sup>e</sup> série
 | language = French
 | pages = 273–286
 | title = Note sur le problème de l'aiguille et le jeu du joint couvert
 | url = http://portail.mathdoc.fr/JMPA/PDF/JMPA_1860_2_5_A18_0.pdf
 | volume = 5
 | year = 1860}}.</ref> In this paper he also presented a solution to [[Buffon's needle problem]], known as [[Buffon's noodle]], that avoided the use of integrals.

He began teaching at a lycée in [[Nice]], but it was not a success, and he soon moved to a position as an assistant astronomer at the [[Paris Observatory]]. He left there in 1865, and in 1880 [[Joseph Louis François Bertrand]] found him in the [[Charenton (asylum)|Charenton asylum]]. Bertrand arranged for Barbier's support and encouraged him to return to mathematical publication.<ref name="mactutor"/>

In this later period of his work, he published ten more papers.<ref name="mactutor"/> He contributed to Bertrand's studies of [[combinatorics]],<ref>{{citation
 | editor1-last = Heyde | editor1-first = C. C.
 | editor1-link= Chris Heyde
 | editor2-last = Seneta | editor2-first = Eugene
 | editor2-link=Eugene Seneta
 | isbn = 978-0-387-95283-3
 | page = 186
 | publisher = Springer
 | title = Statisticians of the Centuries
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=uS3dq_grwr0C&pg=PA186
 | year = 2001}}.</ref> and announced a generalization of [[Bertrand's ballot theorem]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Addario-Berry | first1 = L.
 | last2 = Reed | first2 = B. A. | author2-link = Bruce Reed (mathematician)
 | contribution = Ballot theorems, old and new
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-77200-2_1
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 2432525
 | pages = 9–35
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Bolyai Soc. Math. Stud.
 | title = Horizons of combinatorics
 | volume = 17
 | year = 2008| isbn = 978-3-540-77199-9
 }}.</ref>
He was given the Francoeur Prize for his mathematical research by the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in multiple years.<ref>{{citation
 | journal = The American Naturalist
 | pages = 750–752
 | title = Scientific News
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=JDDyAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA751
 | volume = 18
 | issue = 7
 | year = 1884
 | doi=10.1086/273730| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | date = January 15, 1886
 | issue = 154
 | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]]
 | pages = 49–51
 | title = Notes and News
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Qi8WAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA58
 | doi = 10.1126/science.ns-7.154.49-a
 | volume = 7}}.</ref>

Barbier died on 28 January 1889 in [[Saint-Genest-Lerpt|Saint-Genest]], [[Loire]].<ref name="mactutor"/>
